claim: SRC-107 states that about eleven lapis lazuli deposits are known worldwide, attributing the count to its own reference [16], and names Afghanistan, Siberia, Chile and North America as the important mines with Ariccia (Italy), Mogok (Myanmar) and the Chagai Hills (Pakistan) as smaller ones. SRC-106 and SRC-108 separately name Sar-e Sang (Badakhshan), Lyadjuar Dara (Tajikistan), Lake Baikal, the Urals, Chile, Canada and Vesuvius as provenances entering analytical comparison.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction, chunk 1 ('There are mainly 11 deposits of lapis lazuli that have been found around the world'); SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunks 14-15; SRC-108 INTRODUCTION chunk 1
notes: VERIFIED as a statement of what these publications say. The count of eleven is attributed by SRC-107 to its reference [16], which is not in the retrieved passages and cannot be checked here; the proposition 'there are eleven deposits in the world' is therefore not itself verified. This claim is the first half of the owner's first trap: the alternatives to Badakhshan exist, are named in print, and are numerous. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. Reworded so that each source is cited only for what it says itself, and so that three source identifiers on one row cannot be read as three confirmations. The eleven-deposit count is SRC-107's, attributed by it to a reference that could not be retrieved; and SRC-107 and SRC-106 are not independent for this purpose, since SRC-107 assesses SRC-106 (DRB-008, DEP-036).

claim: The most recent analytical protocol named in the retrieved literature discriminates among four sampled provenances only - Ovalle (Chile), Lyadjuar Dara (Tajikistan), Badakhshan (Afghanistan) and Lake Baikal (Siberia) - which is fewer than the number of candidate ancient sources at DRB-001.
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14: 'The protocol was based on the study and analysis of four main provenances: Ovalle (Chile), Liadjura-Dara or Lojvar Dara (Tajikistan), Badakhshan (Afghanistan) and Lake Baikal (Siberia)', citing Lo Giudice et al. 2017 and Guidorzi et al. 2023
notes: Read together with DRM-002 this is the whole of the first trap. A protocol built on four sampled sources can only ever return one of those four. Chagai, Mogok, Ariccia, the Urals and the North American occurrences are not in it, so an object from any of them would be assigned to whichever of the four it most resembles.

claim: The three published discriminating markers are stated as exclusions rather than identifications: absence of wollastonite indicates Tajikistan, Afghanistan or Siberia; absence of altered pyrite and of Sr in diopside indicates Tajikistan or Afghanistan; a higher Ni/Cu ratio in pyrite indicates Afghanistan (Badakhshan).
locator: SRC-106 chunk 13, the three bulleted markers, citing Guidorzi et al. 2023 and Lo Giudice et al. 2017
notes: Only the third marker is stated positively, and only it distinguishes Afghanistan from Tajikistan. The first two narrow a field of four to three and then to two. A published protocol whose discriminating power rests on one ratio in one mineral phase is a thinner instrument than the phrase 'chemical fingerprint' suggests.

claim: Lapis provenance studies are, in the field's own summary, 'extensively debated but not solved', and most have focused on the Sar-e Sang deposits while 'rarely considering the close exploitable sources in Pakistan and Tajikistan'.
locator: SRC-108 INTRODUCTION chunk 1
notes: A statement about the distribution of research attention, published inside the field, in Archaeometry. It is the mechanism behind the trap rather than an accusation about it: Badakhshan is best characterised partly because it has been studied most, and being best characterised makes it the most available match.

claim: The Chagai Hills are retained as a candidate lapis source in the literature although the deposit's existence is doubted; as reported, Law 2014 holds it 'neither documented nor supported by geological data' and suggests that rock samples associated with Chagai came from the Badakhshan quarries.
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14
notes: Chagai is the principal rival to Badakhshan for the eastern Iranian plateau material, and it is the one whose reference samples are said to be misattributed Badakhshan.

claim: In the retrieved reasoning, the elimination of Chagai as a distinct source proceeds by re-attributing its reference samples to Badakhshan, after which Badakhshan becomes the most probable source: 'If the Chagai's data might be more likely from Badakhshan, then Badakhshan (and especially Sar-e Sang) is the most probably rock resource for the Iranian Plateau.'
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14, final sentence
notes: Recorded as a description of an inferential structure, not as an accusation of error. The re-attribution has a stated evidential basis - sulphur-isotope overlap between the Chagai Hills samples and Afghan ones - and may well be right. What the record notes is the shape of the consequence: the rival source is removed by reassigning its reference material to the favoured source, and the reference set then contains one fewer alternative for every future study. That is how a field converges, and it is also how a field can converge on a wrong answer, and nothing retrieved here distinguishes the two cases.

claim: The Persepolis object data and the reference data they are compared with are not method-commensurable: the objects were powdered and measured by WD-XRF, the reference set was measured by PGAA on whole rock without pre-treatment, and the authors themselves attribute the observed divergence to that difference rather than to source.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 13: 'The reason of variation of Persepolitan samples with different sources could be due to the process of analysis used by Zoldfoldi and Kasztovszky ... as they used PGAA on whole rock without pretreatment while the Persepolitan samples are completely powdered and analysed by WDXRF'
notes: This is stated by the authors and is the strongest single reason not to promote DRB-010 above PROVISIONAL. When the object plots outside every reference cluster and the explanation offered is instrumental, the comparison has not been made.

claim: A 2025 study assessing the Persepolis work holds that its mineralogical characterisation 'was not very informative for provenance, as the Asian lapis lazuli sources that are generally taken into account do not show significant differences in their mineralogy'.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction chunk 5
notes: The next paper to cite the Persepolis study downgrades its central instrument. Recorded under step 11, current standing: the strongest published claim on this material is not the field's settled reading of it two years later.

claim: A companion study of four lapis pieces from the Bronze Age stone-working workshop at Konar Sandal South (Jiroft plain, Iran) 'produced inconclusive results when compared to data from reference rock samples obtained in other studies using PIXE'.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction chunk 5
notes: A second instance of DRB-007's problem, at a different site and with a different technique pairing (SEM-EDS against PIXE). Cross-technique comparison against other laboratories' reference data is where these studies fail, and it fails twice in the retrieved record.

claim: SRC-106 concludes that the lapis of the five Persepolis cylinders came from Badakhshan, on the correlation of pyrite Ni/Cu ratios with Afghan samples and the absence of wollastonite.
locator: SRC-106 CONCLUSIONS chunk 16 and RESULTS chunk 14
notes: One study; its reference comparison is method-incommensurable by its own account (DRB-007); its mineralogy is judged uninformative by the next paper to use it (DRB-008); its rival source was eliminated by reassignment (DRB-006); and the supplementary data behind the pyrite Ni/Cu marker were not delivered by the passage-level lane (SRC-105). The Ni/Cu marker is the one line of evidence not so qualified, and it is why this is PROVISIONAL rather than HYPOTHESIS. Not promotable without the article and its figures. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. Reworded to the reported form so that it stands in the same voice as DRR-001, the corresponding result from the higher-standing study. The first version stated the Iranian study's central result as a bare proposition and set it PROVISIONAL, while stating the US study's central result in the reported form and setting it VERIFIED - a status difference manufactured by the choice of wording and running in exactly the direction BF-028 admits. The row stays PROVISIONAL, because what it reports is a conclusion whose supporting data were not delivered; the equivalent qualification on DRR-001 is carried in its own notes and at DEP-030.

claim: The Persepolis study states, in the same article, both that 'the available data are not sufficient to prove their origin' and that a finding 'proves that the Persepolitan lapis lazuli objects share a provenance with others from Afghanistan (Badakhshan)'.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 11 ('Although the present study shows a probable trade ... the available data are not sufficient to prove their origin'), chunk 12 (the same sentence repeated as a standalone), and chunk 14 ('Accordingly, this finding proves that ...')
notes: A textual observation about one article, recorded and not adjudicated. Both sentences were retrieved. The unit does not claim the authors contradicted themselves in substance - the first sentence concerns the trace-element comparison and the third concerns the pyrite Ni/Cu ratio, and those are different evidence - but the article's own summary language moves from insufficiency to proof within a few pages, and a reader taking only the conclusion would carry away the second and not the first. That gap is how a PROVISIONAL result becomes a citable certainty downstream, which is the mechanism step 11 exists to catch.

claim: That the lapis worked at Shahr-i Sokhta came from Badakhshan.
locator: SRC-106 chunks 11, 12, 13, citing Casanova 1992, Casanova 1998 and Law 2014
notes: The retrieved account is internally divided. Casanova's atomic-absorption Ba/Sr data place the majority of Shahr-i Sokhta samples with Sar-e Sang, Badakhshan and Pamir but relate others to Chagai; SRC-106 chunk 11 reports the earlier reading that the provenance 'may be more likely from Chagai (Pakistan)'; the sulphur-isotope evidence for Badakhshan is reported as resting on ONE sample from the site. One sample is not a provenance for a site with, on the same source's account, large-scale bead production.

claim: SRC-106 reports that Darius's foundation charter for the Apadana at Susa (DSf), written in Old Persian, Akkadian and Elamite, names Sogdiana - not Badakhshan - as the place from which lapis lazuli and carnelian were brought.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 15, citing Basello 2012 and Kent 1953
notes: The clearest case in this unit of a textual provenance label that is not a geological source and must not be read as one. Sar-e Sang is in eastern Bactria, not Sogdiana; the retrieved study reconciles the two by arguing that Sogdians had access to the Sar-e Sang mines. Whether or not that reconciliation is right, the inscription states who supplied, not where the rock formed, and those are two of the owner's ten fields. | REWORDED for status discipline: what is VERIFIED is that the named source states this, with the locator given. The underlying proposition about the world was not independently checked here and, on a single source, would be PROVISIONAL at best.

claim: The Ajanta lapis pigment study dates the murals it sampled to 'the 2nd century bce'.
locator: SRC-107 abstract chunk 0 and chunk 1

The date matters because it decides whether the object belongs to a Blue Road argument at all: a second-century BCE Deccan wall painting and a fifth-century CE one sit in different corridors. HOLD-010 records what is needed - an excavation or epigraphic authority for the painted phase of the caves sampled.

claim: That the lapis pigment at Ajanta came from Sar-e Sang, Badakhshan.
locator: SRC-107 abstract chunk 0, Conclusions chunk 14

The finding may be right; the argument as retrieved does not establish it. Also carries the unresolved date at DRB-014.

claim: Four possible movement paths for that vessel are named in the literature - the Meluhhan, the Marhashian, the Dilmunite-Elamite and the Ananite - and the author declines to call them routes: 'we simply cannot establish the detailed itineraries that might have been followed on the ground'.

Note that all four are named from Mesopotamian toponyms, so even the vocabulary for describing a movement between Arabia and Central Asia is borrowed from the archive of a third region. APA-R-003.

claim: SRC-121 states that the fundamental assumption of scientific provenance studies is Damour's of 1865 - that an object whose material is of distant or foreign origin implies transport of the object, or at least of the matter it is formed from - and that the concept 'has essentially gone unchallenged since 1865'.
locator: SRC-121 chunk 1, quoting Damour 1865: 313 in French with an English translation
notes: The dated warrant behind the whole domain, and the reason the three-claim rule is not a stylistic preference. Damour's inference licenses a conclusion about the movement of matter and about nothing else. Every step from matter to people, and from people to language, is an additional inference that Damour does not supply and that must be evidenced separately. BR-R-001 to BR-R-003. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. The first version asserted as a bare world-proposition that this inference underlies EVERY provenance claim on both roads - a universal quantifier over the whole domain, at VERIFIED, on a single passage. Reworded to the reported form, which is what the passage supports. The substantive use made of it is unaffected: BR-R-001 accepts the material-to-movement bridge on this warrant and fixes its scope to what the warrant covers.

claim: Canonical discriminant analysis 'assumes that the dataset being evaluated contains all possible groups', so an artefact 'will be assigned membership in the group it most closely resembles even if the group (source) to which it actually belongs is not present in the dataset'.
locator: SRC-109 EVALUATION OF THE RESULTS, chunk 13, final paragraph
notes: Stated by the analysts themselves, about their own method. This is the general form of the owner's first trap and it governs both roads: an unsampled source is not a weak match, it is invisible, and its objects are silently distributed among the sources that were sampled. Read with DRB-002 it means that a four-source lapis protocol cannot report 'none of these'.

claim: Increasing the density of geological sampling is expected to REDUCE the apparent separation between sources, not improve it; the authors of one reference dataset 'anticipated that additional geochemical data from geological samples would probably lead to more overlaps between sources'.
locator: SRC-122 DISCUSSION
notes: The counter-intuitive half of DRM-002, and the more dangerous one. Apparent discrimination between sources can be an artefact of thin sampling, so a protocol that separates four lapis sources cleanly is not thereby shown to be a good instrument; it may be showing the gaps in its own reference set. The same passage adds that geological samples collected to answer geological questions cannot simply be reused as provenance comparison material, because the sampling criteria differ.

claim: In the wider sourcing literature 'some artefacts reported in the literature have been assigned to quarries based on one published geochemical analysis for a particular source', and source characterisations built on second-hand collections rather than field sampling carry Type I and Type II error risks the analyst 'may not even be aware' of.
locator: SRC-123 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS; SRC-124 'The chemical characterization of stone: beyond fishing expeditions'
notes: Both statements are about lithic sourcing generally - Polynesian basalt and North American chert - and neither is about lapis or carnelian. Carried as general statements about the practice and labelled as such, because they name the exact conditions the lapis reference sets meet: small samples, and museum or merchant material standing in for field collection (DRR-004).

claim: SRC-126 reports that beads from the third-millennium stone-working workshop at Konar Sandal (Jiroft) previously 'identified as calcite' on the artefacts' appearance were shown by micro-Raman, micro-XRF, FTIR and XRD to be gypsum alabaster - a material attribution made from appearance, overturned by analysis.
locator: SRC-126 abstract and Discussion
notes: The plainest available demonstration that the museum-candidate register's material column is a hypothesis and not a datum. It is also on the Blue Road's own ground - Konar Sandal is in the Halil Rud, the region most often proposed for Marhashi - and the same site's lapis produced inconclusive provenance results (DRB-009). | REWORDED for status discipline: what is VERIFIED is that the named source states this, with the locator given. The underlying proposition about the world was not independently checked here and, on a single source, would be PROVISIONAL at best.

claim: Of 791 texts in the CDLI corpus naming at least one of Meluhha, Magan, Dilmun and Marhashi, 742 - 93.8% - name exactly one; 38 name two, 10 name three, and one text names all four.
locator: 04-AUDITS/domain-r-cdli-distributions.py CO-OCCURRENCE section over 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, counting only the classifications PLACE-DETERMINATIVE, LAND-DETERMINATIVE, UNMARKED and PERSON-OF; the four-name text is P469516, catalogued Old Babylonian, provenience Nippur
notes: The owner's fourth trap answered with a number rather than an assurance. The four are, in the surviving record, overwhelmingly named apart. Pairwise: Magan with Meluhha in 38 texts, Dilmun with Magan in 12, Dilmun with Meluhha in 11, Marhashi with Meluhha in 9, Dilmun with Marhashi in 3, Magan with Marhashi in 2. The familiar triad of Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha - which is how modern synthesis almost always introduces them - stands in nine of 863 texts. Marhashi is the most separate of the four. | CORRECTED after the preferred-counter-narrative test (BF-030). The first draft of this row let the 94.2% carry an argument it cannot carry. A text naming one toponym is not evidence that its writer held the four apart: most of the 863 are short administrative documents in which only one place is at issue, and a receipt naming Magan had no occasion to name Dilmun. What the figure measures is the shape of the surviving record, not ancient conceptual practice. It is still the right answer to the trap, because the trap is about OUR practice: the modern synthesis introduces the four as a set, and the record it draws on presents them as a set in nine texts out of 863. The claim is about where the grouping comes from, and the answer is that it comes from a small number of royal and literary texts and not from the administrative mass. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. The base was 863 texts and 813 singletons before two classifier repairs: the Dilmun unit of account (BF-032) and the non-toponymic determinatives on the other three toponyms (BF-033). Both moved the denominator. The proportion barely changed, 94.2% to 93.8%, which is the one reassuring thing about the correction and is not a reason to have skipped it.

claim: A toponym written in cuneiform is not one kind of thing, and this holds for all four. me-luh-ha carries the land determinative {kur}, the place determinative {ki}, the bird determinative {muszen} in the lexical bird name dar-meluhha, and wood terms, and stands as a personal-name element in dumu me-luh-ha. Once the same screen is run on the other three: 115 occurrences of ma2-gan carry the timber determinative {gesz}, 4 of dilmun carry the bronze determinative {zabar}, 3 are divine names, and 1 of mar-ha-szi carries the vegetable determinative {sar} in szum2-sikil mar-ha-szi{sar}, an onion.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, classifications TIMBER-DETERMINATIVE (115 MAGAN), METAL-DETERMINATIVE (4 DILMUN), DIVINE-NAME (2 MAGAN, 1 DILMUN), VEGETABLE-DETERMINATIVE (1 MARHASI), BIRD-DETERMINATIVE (4 MELUHHA), plus 67 LAND-DETERMINATIVE and 20 PLACE-DETERMINATIVE for MELUHHA and 23 BOUND-IN-COMPOUND-OR-NAME
notes: A textual provenance label is not one kind of thing. The same sequence names a land, a place, a bird, two timbers and a person. Reading every occurrence as a reference to a region overstates the toponym by roughly a quarter of its occurrences, and the wood and bird uses are the ones a materials domain is most likely to mistake for evidence of trade in a material. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. The first version ran this screen for Meluhha alone, and asserted in its note that reading every occurrence as a region 'overstates the toponym' - a claim it had tested for one of four names. Running it on the other three found 123 further occurrences that are not the toponym, of which the largest group by far is Magan-timber. The generalisation was true; it had not been measured. BF-033.

claim: The determinative on Meluhha shifts with period, and the genres on the two sides of the shift are not symmetrical. In third-millennium and Old Babylonian texts it takes the place determinative {ki} - 20 occurrences, none with {kur} - spread across Girsu (5), Ur (5), Nippur (5), Umma, Irisagrig and three of unrecorded findspot, in texts of mixed genre: administrative, royal-inscriptional, lexical and literary. In Neo-Assyrian texts it takes the land determinative {kur} - 67 occurrences, none with {ki}, all Neo-Assyrian, 64 at Nineveh and 3 at Assur - in royal itineraries and titulature.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, target MELUHHA, classifications PLACE-DETERMINATIVE and LAND-DETERMINATIVE cross-tabulated by cdli_period and cdli_provenience; representative {ki} lines i3-dub e2-duru5-me-luh-ha{ki} (P108484, administrative, Girsu) and _ma2_ me-luh-ha{ki} (P461937, royal inscription); representative {kur} lines a-na {kur}ma2-kan-na u {kur}me-luh-ha lu-u al-lik (P392229) and _lugal_ {kur}me-luh-ha (P392594)
notes: A measured orthographic change accompanying a change of genre and of place of writing, across roughly 1,400 years. This unit does NOT assert what the Neo-Assyrian word denotes; it records that the referent cannot be assumed constant, and that a corridor argument built on 'Meluhha' must say which Meluhha it means. The standard identification of the first-millennium term with Nubia is not retrieved here and is not asserted; HOLD-009. | CORRECTED 2026-09-09 after independent adversarial review. The first version said the {ki} occurrences were 'chiefly at Girsu' in 'granary and personnel records'. Neither holds: Girsu ties with Ur and Nippur at five each, and the set includes the moored-ships royal inscription that DRM-017 itself discusses, two Lagash II inscriptions, two lexical entries and several literary passages. The contrast between the two halves is real in the determinative, the period and the place of writing; it is NOT a clean administrative-versus-royal contrast, and the first version manufactured one.

The designation occurs in 13 rows across 10 texts: 12 rows in 9 texts catalogued Ur III at Girsu, and one row at P467759, catalogued Old Akkadian, from Ur.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, target MELUHHA: ki ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha-ta (P102519), ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha (P108448, twice), dumu me-luh-ha and dumu [me-luh-ha] (P123177), x ur-{d}ig-alim dumu me-luh-ha (P124739), dumu me-luh-ha erin2 e2 {d}nansze-ta (P135727), kiszib3 ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha (P136196), P202783 twice, P207485, P318542, and dumu# me-luh-ha (P467759, Old Akkadian, Ur)
notes: Directly on the owner's three-claim rule and retrieved from the primary corpus rather than argued. Whether dumu me-luh-ha is an ethnic designation or a patronymic on a personal name Meluhha is not settled by the phrase, and both readings are live. Under either, the name actually borne is Sumerian and theophoric. A person carrying a foreign toponym as a designation is not thereby a speaker of a foreign language, and this is the case in the record where that can be seen rather than assumed. BR-R-003. | CORRECTED after the preferred-counter-narrative test (BF-030). The first draft treated the Sumerian names as though they showed something about what these people spoke.
